item.title: A calmer way to read the web
item.author: mara@example.com (Mara Bell)
item.description:
The web is still at its best when it feels like a library: quiet, durable, and yours to explore.

Keep the useful parts close

rxs saves downloaded articles in a local SQLite database, so a train tunnel or flaky connection never interrupts your reading list.

  • Move quickly with familiar keyboard shortcuts.
  • Search titles and downloaded article text.
  • Star useful stories and return to them later.

Make room for attention

A reading queue should help you decide what deserves your time without demanding attention of its own. A focused interface keeps subscriptions, headlines, and the current story close without turning them into a dashboard.

Keyboard navigation makes that rhythm predictable. Filter the feed list, move through downloaded stories, and open one in a reader that gives the text the whole terminal.

Own the quiet moments

Local storage also makes the small moments useful. Articles remain ready on a commute, during a flight, or anywhere the network is unreliable. Reading progress stays with the article, so it is easy to leave and return later.

The result is deliberately modest: no account, no algorithmic timeline, and no pressure to keep scrolling. Just the writing you chose to follow.

Feeds stay simple, portable, and available offline. Read more about local-first software.

item.title: Building a durable reading queue
item.author: mara@example.com (Mara Bell)
item.description:
A useful reading queue is fast to search, easy to back up, and available without a network connection.

Keeping subscriptions and articles in SQLite makes those properties the default instead of an optional sync mode.

item.title: Your subscriptions should be portable
item.author: mara@example.com (Mara Bell)
item.description: OPML keeps a list of feeds independent from any one reader. Export it, keep a copy, and take it wherever you read next.
